title: Export Production-Ready Assets from Figma
seoTitle: Figma to Production Assets — SVG, PNG Export Settings and Optimization
seoDescription: Export clean SVG and PNG assets from Figma for web, iOS, Android, and print. Outline text, flatten effects, optimize file size, and avoid common export failures.
content: # Export Production-Ready Assets from Figma Figma exports look perfect in preview but break in production for predictable reasons: live text that references unavailable fonts, effects that flatten to raster, masks that create clipping artifacts, and absolute positioning that fails responsive layouts. This guide walks through export settings that produce assets engineers can use without manual cleanup. ## Why Vectroy for Figma Assets? Post-Export Optimization: Clean up Figma's verbose SVG output—remove editor metadata, collapse groups, reduce decimal precision. Batch Processing: Export an entire icon set, optimize all files in one pass, and verify they still render correctly. Web-Ready Output: Inline critical CSS, remove Figma's default viewBox padding, and ensure assets work in all browsers. ## Figma Export Checklist 1. **Outline Text**: Convert all text layers to outlines before export (Cmd+Shift+O). Fonts render differently across platforms. 2. **Flatten Effects**: Shadows, blurs, and blend modes don't export reliably. Use "Flatten" to rasterize them into the base layer. 3. **Simplify Paths**: Reduce node count with the "Simplify" command (Cmd+Shift+P) to shrink file size. 4. **Name Layers**: Export names come from layer names. Use descriptive, kebab-case names (icon-home, button-primary). 5. **Set Export Scale**: @1x for web SVG, @2x and @3x for mobile PNG, 300 DPI for print PDF. ## SVG Export Settings Figma's SVG export dialog has three critical settings: - **Include "id" attribute**: Disable unless you're animating with JavaScript. IDs add bulk and create conflicts when multiple instances load. - **Outline text**: Always enable. Keeps text editable in Figma but exports as paths. - **Simplify stroke**: Enable for icons, disable for illustrations. Converts strokes to fills, which reduces nodes but loses stroke-width editability. ## PNG Export for High-DPI Screens Mobile apps need @2x and @3x assets. Export at 2× and 3× scale in Figma, then name files with suffixes: `icon-home@2x.png`, `icon-home@3x.png`. iOS and Android asset catalogs read these suffixes automatically. For web, export @2x PNG and serve via `srcset`: ``. This gives Retina displays crisp rendering without forcing all users to download large files. ## PDF Export for Print Figma's PDF export is RGB, not CMYK. For print-ready files, export as SVG, open in Illustrator, convert to CMYK, and add bleed. Or export a high-res PNG (600 DPI) and embed it in a print-ready PDF with proper crop marks. ## Common Export Failures Text Renders as Boxes: Font not available on the target platform. Outline text before export, or embed the font (increases file size). Effects Disappear: Shadow or blur didn't export. Flatten the effect into the base layer before export. Mask Clips Unexpectedly: Figma's masks use CSS clip-path, which older browsers don't support. Flatten masked layers into a single shape. Colors Look Different: Figma uses display P3 color space; most web browsers use sRGB. Export with "Convert to sRGB" enabled. ## Icon Sets and Batch Export For icon libraries, use Figma's batch export: select all frames, set export settings once, and export all at once. Name each frame consistently (icon-name-variant), and Figma will name files accordingly. After export, use Vectroy's batch optimizer to reduce file size across the entire set without manual tweaking. ## Responsive SVG Sizing Figma exports SVG with fixed width/height attributes. For responsive web SVG, remove those attributes and rely on viewBox only. The SVG will scale to fit its container. Or set `width="100%" height="auto"` in the exported file. ## Troubleshooting If exported SVG looks different from Figma preview, check for blend modes (Multiply, Overlay) that CSS doesn't support well—flatten them. If file size is huge, check for embedded raster images—export those separately as PNG. If edges look pixelated, increase export scale (2× or 4×), then scale down in CSS with image-rendering: crisp-edges.

title: Vectorize and Export Logo Variants for Branding

content:
# Vectorize and Export Logo Variants for Branding

A logo's value lies not in a single file but in a system of variants. Horizontal, vertical, stacked, monochrome, and inverted versions must all work at favicon size and billboard scale. This guide walks through vectorizing logos in Figma, creating consistent variants, and exporting specs that production teams can follow.

## Vectorization Fundamentals

If you're redesigning a raster logo or importing a sketch, start with vectorization. Figma's **Image Trace** (Image > Trace) converts raster to vector paths, but quality depends on the source. For hand-drawn logos:

1. **Prepare the raster**: High contrast, remove background noise, and ensure clean edges before tracing.
2. **Adjust trace settings**: Experiment with **Threshold** (controls detail) and **Tolerance** (smooths paths). Higher tolerance = simpler paths, smaller file size.
3. **Review and refine**: Trace produces rough output. Manually simplify paths with the Pen tool, remove redundant nodes, and ensure consistent stroke weights.
4. **Test at small sizes**: Export at 16px to verify the logo remains legible as a favicon.

## Creating Logo Variants

Every logo system needs at least these variants:

- **Horizontal (lockup)**: Logo + wordmark side-by-side. Standard use case.
- **Stacked (vertical)**: Logo above wordmark. Used in narrow layouts (mobile, sidebars).
- **Icon only**: Logo without wordmark. For favicons, app icons, social media avatars.
- **Monochrome (black)**: Single-color version. For embroidery, etching, minimal contexts.
- **Monochrome (white)**: Inverted for dark backgrounds. Required for print, merchandise.
- **Outline**: Stroke-only version for cut vinyl or laser applications.

Build each variant as a component in Figma with consistent naming: `logo-horizontal`, `logo-stacked`, `logo-icon`, `logo-mono-black`, `logo-mono-white`, `logo-outline`.

## Stroke Consistency and Pixel Alignment

For logos with strokes, consistency is critical:

- **Stroke weight**: Choose one (commonly 2px for web, 1.5pt for print). Apply uniformly across all elements.
- **Stroke alignment**: Set to **Center** for predictable scaling. Inner/Outer alignment can cause misalignment at small sizes.
- **Pixel alignment**: Enable **Pixel Snapping** in Figma export settings. Prevents anti-aliasing artifacts.
- **Corner radius**: Use consistent corner styles (rounded vs sharp) to reinforce brand identity.

## Export Specifications

Create an export manifest for your brand guidelines:

**SVG (Web)**: Horizontal, stacked, icon at 1x. Outline text if wordmark includes type.

**PNG (App/Social)**: Icon variant at @1x, @2x, @3x (16px, 32px, 48px; 128px, 256px, 512px for social).

**PDF (Print)**: All variants at 300 DPI. Include full-color, monochrome, and knockout (white-on-dark) versions.

**Minimum size**: Test all variants at 16px. If icon breaks legibility, redesign or document size restrictions.

## Brand Guideline Asset Prep

When exporting for guidelines, include:

1. **Clear space**: Minimum padding around the logo. Mark as a dotted box in Figma, export with guides.
2. **Size restrictions**: Minimum width in pixels (e.g., "never smaller than 80px on web").
3. **Color specs**: Export the primary brand color as hex, RGB, and Pantone (if print).
4. **Incorrect usage**: Create a variant showing common mistakes (stretched, rotated, modified colors). This prevents future misuse.
5. **File organization**: Export to folders by type: `horizontal/`, `stacked/`, `icon/`, `monochrome/`, `print/`.

## Testing and Delivery

Before finalizing:

- **Scale test**: Export at 16px, 32px, 64px, 256px. Verify legibility at all sizes.
- **Format test**: SVG in browsers (Chrome, Safari, Firefox), PNG in all applications.
- **Color accuracy**: Print a proof. RGB-to-CMYK conversion can shift colors significantly.
- **File naming**: Use consistent, version-controlled names (`logo-v2-horizontal-color.svg`, not `logo_final_FINAL_2.svg`).

Deliver as a Figma project with shared library access for teams. Export all variants into a zip file with a README documenting sizes, color values, and usage restrictions.

title: Build a Consistent Icon System in Figma
seoTitle: Icon System Design — Grid Alignment, Stroke Consistency, SVG Optimization
seoDescription: Design icon systems with consistent grids, stroke weights, sizing conventions, and naming. Export optimized SVGs for production use.
content: # Build a Consistent Icon System in Figma Icon systems live or die on consistency. A 24px icon drawn on a 16px grid, paired with inconsistent stroke weights, fragments across products. This guide covers grid setup, stroke standardization, naming conventions, and SVG export best practices for production icon libraries. ## Grid and Size Standards Start with a grid and stick to it. Common conventions: - **Web**: 16px, 24px, 32px base sizes (commonly increased to 48px, 64px for touch interfaces). - **Mobile**: 24px, 48px (iOS), 24px, 48px (Android). - **Desktop app**: 16px (UI elements), 32px (toolbar), 64px (app icon). In Figma, set up your artboard at 64px × 64px with a **2px padding** (leaving 60px × 60px for content). This gives buffer space and scales cleanly to 16px (÷4), 24px (×3/8), 32px (÷2). Enable **Pixel Grid** (View > Pixel Grid) and **Guides** to snap all paths to grid. For strokes, enable **Snap to Pixel** in export settings. ## Stroke Weight Consistency All icons in a system must use the same stroke weight. Common standards: - **Thin (1.5px)**: Minimal, modern aesthetic. Works at 24px and above. - **Regular (2px)**: Most versatile. Works at 16px–64px. - **Bold (2.5–3px)**: Emphasizes icons, used sparingly for important states. Choose one primary stroke weight, then optionally offer a bold variant. Apply uniformly: 1. **Stroke alignment**: Center (scales predictably). Never mix inner/outer. 2. **Corner radius**: Consistent joins (rounded vs. sharp). Set caps to **Round** for softer appearance. 3. **Filled vs. outlined**: Separate these into different sets (outlined for default, filled for active/hover states). Verify consistency by toggling between icons at 16px preview. Mismatches stand out immediately. ## Naming Conventions Establish a naming schema before creating 200+ icons. Example: `icon-[name]-[size]-[weight]` - `icon-home-24-regular` - `icon-menu-24-bold` - `icon-chevron-right-16-regular` Or, if size and weight are uniform across your set: `icon-[descriptive-name]` (e.g., `icon-home`, `icon-menu`, `icon-chevron-right`) In Figma, organize as components with **variant properties**: - Base component: `icon` - Variant 1: `name=home|size=24|state=default` - Variant 2: `name=home|size=24|state=filled` This makes swapping variants in designs instant for design teams. ## Testing at Actual Sizes Before exporting: 1. **Preview at target sizes**: Export a test set at 16px, 24px, 32px. Open in browser or image viewer. Legibility drops off fast at 16px. 2. **Check antialiasing**: Zoom to 100% in your browser. Look for rough edges or misaligned strokes. If evident, enable **Pixel Snapping** in Figma. 3. **Contrast test**: Ensure icons work on both light and dark backgrounds. Export a white version on a dark canvas; export dark on light. 4. **Pair with type**: Icons rarely stand alone. Test icons next to text at the size you'll use them. Ensure visual balance. ## SVG Export and Cleanup Figma's SVG export includes editor metadata (IDs, layer names, unused styles). Before shipping: 1. **Export from Figma**: Select icon, right-click > Copy as SVG (or Export > SVG). 2. **Run SVGO**: `svgo icon-home.svg --output icon-home.opt.svg`. Removes metadata, simplifies paths, reduces file size by 30–50%. 3. **Verify rendering**: Open optimized SVG in browser. Compare to original. Some optimization may strip essential data; adjust SVGO config if needed. 4. **Inline or link**: For web, inline SVGs in CSS `background-image` or use ``. Inline gives more styling control; linked keeps markup clean. ## Organizing and Versioning Store your icon system with clear structure: ``` icon-system/ ├── figma/ (source file) ├── src/ │ ├── 16px/ │ ├── 24px/ │ ├── 32px/ │ └── 64px/ ├── dist/ (optimized SVG) ├── package.json (version, metadata) └── README.md (usage guide) ``` Version your icon set (e.g., v1.0, v1.1, v2.0). When adding new icons, increment minor version; breaking changes (renamed icons, grid changes) bump major. Publish to npm or a private package registry for easy consumption. ## Integration with Design Tools For design teams, set up Figma components with auto-layout: 1. Create a 24px × 24px component frame. 2. Add the icon path inside. 3. Set auto-layout with 0 padding and no spacing. 4. Enable **Resizable**: All selected (so designs can scale the component). 5. Publish to a Figma library for team access. Designers can now drag icons into designs, resize instantly, and stay in sync when you publish updates.

title: Optimize Fonts for Web Performance
seoTitle: Font Optimization — Subsetting, Variable Fonts, WOFF2 Conversion
seoDescription: Optimize fonts for web with subsetting, variable fonts, and WOFF2 format. Reduce file sizes, check licenses, and implement Google Fonts best practices.
content:
# Optimize Fonts for Web Performance

Web fonts slow pages down. A full font family at 400–800 KB per weight shifts layouts, delays text rendering, and burns mobile data. This guide covers subsetting, variable fonts, format conversion, and licensing checks to ship fonts that load fast.

## Why Font File Size Matters

Every font weight is a separate HTTP request. A typical family (regular, medium, bold, italic) is 2–3 MB uncompressed. On slow networks:

- **FOIT (Flash of Invisible Text)**: Text stays invisible until fonts load.
- **FOUT (Flash of Unstyled Text)**: System font shows first, then swaps. Creates jarring layout shift.
- **Cumulative Layout Shift**: Text reflows when font loads, breaking scroll position.

Subsetting and compression reduce load time from 2–3s to 200–400ms, making text instantly readable.

## Subsetting Fonts

Subsetting removes unused glyphs. A Latin-only site doesn't need Cyrillic, Greek, or CJK characters. Subsetting a font to Latin + punctuation cuts file size by 60–80%.

### Using Glyphhanger

```bash
# Install glyphhanger (requires Node.js)
npm install -g glyphhanger

# Subset a font to Latin only
glyphhanger --LATIN --subset=font.ttf

# Subset to specific text (for headings)
glyphhanger --whitelist="ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ0123456789" --subset=heading.ttf
```

### Using Fonttools (Python)

```bash
# Install fonttools
pip install fonttools brotli

# Subset to Latin
pyftsubset font.ttf \
  --output-file=font-subset.woff2 \
  --flavor=woff2 \
  --layout-features='*' \
  --unicodes=U+0000-00FF,U+0131,U+0152-0153,U+02BB-02BC,U+02C6,U+02DA,U+02DC,U+2000-206F,U+2074,U+20AC,U+2122,U+2191,U+2193,U+2212,U+2215,U+FEFF,U+FFFD
```

This reduces a 200 KB TTF to 40–60 KB WOFF2.

## Variable Fonts vs. Static Families

Variable fonts store multiple weights in one file. Instead of 6 files (Thin, Light, Regular, Medium, Bold, Black), one variable font covers 100–900 weight range.

**Pros**:
- Smaller total file size (one 80 KB file vs. six 40 KB files = 240 KB saved).
- Smooth weight transitions (animate from 400 to 700).
- Fewer HTTP requests.

**Cons**:
- Not all fonts offer variable versions.
- Older browsers (IE11) don't support variable fonts (fallback to static).

Use variable fonts when you need 3+ weights. For one or two weights, static fonts are smaller.

## Format Conversion: WOFF2 is King

Font formats by size (same typeface):

- **TTF/OTF**: 200 KB (uncompressed)
- **WOFF**: 120 KB (compressed)
- **WOFF2**: 80 KB (Brotli compression, ~40% smaller than WOFF)

Modern browsers (Chrome, Firefox, Safari, Edge) support WOFF2. Skip WOFF and TTF unless supporting IE11.

### Converting to WOFF2

```bash
# Using fonttools
pyftsubset font.ttf --output-file=font.woff2 --flavor=woff2
```

Or use online tools: [everythingfonts.com](https://everythingfonts.com/), [transfonter.org](https://transfonter.org/).

## Licensing and Legal Compliance

Before subsetting or self-hosting:

1. **Check the license**: Read the font's EULA. Some licenses prohibit modification or self-hosting.
2. **Google Fonts**: Free to subset, modify, and self-host (SIL Open Font License).
3. **Commercial fonts**: Adobe Fonts, MyFonts, Monotype often prohibit subsetting. Check before optimizing.
4. **Embedding permissions**: Some fonts allow web embedding but not subsetting. Verify OTF/TTF embedding bits.

If unsure, email the foundry. Licensing violations risk legal action.

## Google Fonts Best Practices

Google Fonts are pre-optimized but can be further tuned:

### 1. Limit Weights and Styles

```html
<!-- Bad: loads 12 font files -->
<link href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=Inter:wght@100;200;300;400;500;600;700;800;900&display=swap" rel="stylesheet">

<!-- Good: loads 2 files -->
<link href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=Inter:wght@400;700&display=swap" rel="stylesheet">
```

### 2. Self-Host for Performance

Download Google Fonts and serve from your CDN. Eliminates DNS lookup and TLS handshake to fonts.googleapis.com.

```bash
# Download Google Font
curl -o inter.woff2 "https://fonts.gstatic.com/s/inter/v12/UcCO3FwrK3iLTeHuS_fvQtMwCp50KnMw2boKoduKmMEVuLyfAZ9hiA.woff2"
```

Then reference in CSS:

```css
@font-face {
  font-family: 'Inter';
  font-style: normal;
  font-weight: 400;
  src: url('/fonts/inter.woff2') format('woff2');
  font-display: swap;
}
```

### 3. Use `font-display: swap`

Prevents FOIT. Text shows immediately in fallback font, then swaps when custom font loads.

```css
@font-face {
  font-family: 'Inter';
  src: url('/fonts/inter.woff2') format('woff2');
  font-display: swap; /* Critical */
}
```

## Testing and Validation

Before deploying:

- **File size check**: Optimized fonts should be 40–80 KB per weight. If larger, subset more aggressively.
- **Render test**: Open the font in FontDrop (fontdrop.info) to verify glyphs render correctly after subsetting.
- **Cross-browser test**: Test in Chrome, Firefox, Safari. Ensure fallback fonts work in IE11 if supporting it.
- **Lighthouse audit**: Run Google Lighthouse. Fonts should load in <500ms on 3G.

Subsetting, WOFF2 conversion, and self-hosting reduce font load times from seconds to milliseconds, making text instantly readable.

content:
# Organize and Version Design Assets

Brand assets scatter across drives, Figma files, and local folders until no one knows which logo is current. This guide covers folder structure, naming conventions, version control, and asset libraries that keep brand files organized, accessible, and up-to-date.

## Folder Structure

Start with a clear hierarchy. Two common approaches:

### Type-Based Structure

```
brand-assets/
├── logos/
│   ├── horizontal/
│   ├── stacked/
│   ├── icon/
│   └── archive/
├── colors/
│   ├── palette.pdf
│   └── tokens.json
├── typography/
│   ├── fonts/
│   └── specimens/
├── icons/
├── photography/
├── templates/
│   ├── presentations/
│   ├── social-media/
│   └── print/
└── guidelines/
    └── brand-guide-v3.pdf
```

Pros: Easy to find all logos, colors, or icons in one place.  
Cons: Hard to see all assets for a specific project or campaign.

### Project-Based Structure

```
brand-assets/
├── brand-identity-2024/
│   ├── logos/
│   ├── colors/
│   ├── typography/
│   └── deliverables/
├── website-redesign/
│   ├── mockups/
│   ├── components/
│   └── assets/
├── q1-campaign/
│   ├── social/
│   ├── print/
│   └── email/
└── core-assets/
    ├── logos/
    ├── colors/
    └── fonts/
```

Pros: All assets for a project are together.  
Cons: Core assets (logos, colors) may duplicate across folders.

**Recommendation**: Hybrid. Use type-based for core brand assets (logos, colors, fonts), project-based for campaigns and temporary work.

## Naming Conventions

Inconsistent naming creates chaos. Establish rules before creating 500 files:

### File Naming Schema

```
[asset-type]-[descriptor]-[variant]-[version].[format]

Examples:
logo-horizontal-color-v2.svg
logo-icon-mono-black-v2.png
button-primary-hover-default.svg
icon-home-24-regular.svg
photo-hero-landing-page-2024-q1.jpg
```

### Rules

1. **Lowercase with hyphens**: No spaces, underscores, or camelCase. `logo-horizontal.svg`, not `Logo Horizontal.svg` or `logo_horizontal.svg`.
2. **Descriptive, not generic**: `button-primary-hover.svg`, not `button1.svg`.
3. **Version suffix**: `-v1`, `-v2`, `-v3`. Never `_final`, `_FINAL2`, `_final_REAL`.
4. **Date for time-sensitive assets**: `hero-photo-2024-11.jpg` for assets that expire or get replaced seasonally.
5. **Size/scale in filename for raster**: `icon-home-24.png`, `icon-home-48@2x.png`.

### Figma Layer Naming

Same rules apply in Figma:

- Components: `button/primary`, `icon/home`, `logo/horizontal`
- Variants: `size=24|state=default`, `theme=light|state=hover`
- Frames: `home-hero-desktop-1920`, `dashboard-mobile-375`

Consistent naming makes exports automatic (Export as SVG uses layer name).

## Version Control

Design files need version control just like code.

### For Figma

Figma has built-in version history (File > Show Version History). Use it:

1. **Save versions after major changes**: "Logo finalized", "Color palette updated", "Website redesign complete".
2. **Restore old versions**: Click a version to restore or duplicate it.
3. **Branching**: Create a branch (File > Save as branch) for experimental work. Merge back when approved.

### For Files (Logos, PDFs, Fonts)

Use **Git** or **cloud storage with versioning**:

#### Git (for developers and technical teams)

```bash
# Initialize repo
git init
git add logos/
git commit -m "Add logo variants v2"

# Tag releases
git tag v2.0
git push origin v2.0
```

Pros: Full history, branching, collaboration.  
Cons: Non-designers find Git intimidating.

#### Cloud Storage (Dropbox, Google Drive)

Enable version history:

- **Google Drive**: Right-click > Manage versions. Upload new versions, restore old ones.
- **Dropbox**: File history keeps 30-day (free) or unlimited (paid) history.

Pros: Easy for non-technical teams.  
Cons: No branching, limited comparison tools.

## Asset Libraries

Keep brand assets accessible across teams.

### Figma Libraries

Publish components and styles as a library:

1. **Create a Brand Library file**: Components for logos, buttons, icons, colors, typography.
2. **Publish as library**: Assets > Publish library.
3. **Enable in team files**: Any file in your team can now use components from the library.

When you update the library, Figma prompts designers to accept updates in their files. This keeps everyone on the latest logos/colors without manual copying.

### Cloud-Based Asset Management

For non-Figma assets (photos, fonts, videos):

- **Notion**: Embed files, organize by category, add metadata (license, usage notes).
- **Google Drive**: Shared folders with clear structure. Use Drive File Stream for local sync.
- **Dropbox**: Similar to Drive. Better for large files (video, high-res photos).
- **Abstract** (paid): Version control for Sketch and Adobe XD. Git-like branching for designers.

## Backup Strategy

Design files are irreplaceable. Backup everything:

1. **Cloud sync**: All files in Google Drive, Dropbox, or similar. Auto-syncs from local.
2. **Figma auto-saves**: Figma files live in the cloud. Export critical files as `.fig` backups monthly.
3. **External drive**: Quarterly backup of entire `brand-assets/` folder to external SSD.

If Figma, Drive, or Dropbox fails (rare but possible), you have offline copies.

## Access Control and Permissions

Not everyone needs edit access. Set permissions:

- **View-only**: Marketing, external partners. Can view and download, can't edit.
- **Edit**: Designers, brand managers. Can modify files.
- **Admin**: Creative director. Can delete, change permissions, manage libraries.

In Figma: Share > Set permissions (View, Edit, Admin).  
In Drive/Dropbox: Share > Viewer, Commenter, Editor.

## Archiving Old Assets

Don't delete old assets—archive them. Create an `archive/` folder for superseded logos, outdated colors, or deprecated designs.

Example:

```
logos/
├── current/
│   ├── logo-horizontal-v3.svg
│   └── logo-icon-v3.svg
└── archive/
    ├── logo-horizontal-v1.svg
    ├── logo-horizontal-v2.svg
    └── old-brand-2019/
```

When someone asks "what did the old logo look like?", you have it.

content:
# Figma Dev Mode and Design-to-Code Handoff

Designers hand off Figma files. Developers inspect them, guess at spacing, and rebuild components from scratch. Figma Dev Mode and design tokens eliminate guesswork, turning design specs into production-ready code.

## Figma Dev Mode Basics

Dev Mode (View > Dev Mode, or toggle in top-right) shows developers exactly what they need:

- **CSS for layers**: Copy CSS directly (padding, margin, color, font-size).
- **Asset exports**: Download icons, images at correct scale.
- **Measurements**: Spacing between elements, dimensions, alignment.
- **Component mapping**: Link Figma components to code components (via Code Connect or manual docs).

**For designers**: Before handoff, enable Dev Mode and verify measurements are correct. Use auto-layout for consistent spacing.

**For developers**: Inspect any layer. Copy CSS. Export assets. No guessing.

## Design Tokens: The Bridge Between Design and Code

Design tokens are design decisions stored as data: colors, spacing, typography, shadows, radii. Export them as JSON, then consume in CSS, SCSS, or JavaScript.

### What Gets Tokenized

- **Colors**: `--color-primary: #3B6DFF;`
- **Spacing**: `--space-xs: 4px; --space-sm: 8px; --space-md: 16px;`
- **Typography**: `--font-size-body: 16px; --font-family-sans: 'Inter', sans-serif;`
- **Shadows**: `--shadow-sm: 0 1px 2px rgba(0,0,0,0.05);`
- **Radii**: `--radius-sm: 4px; --radius-md: 8px; --radius-full: 9999px;`

### Why Tokens Matter

Without tokens, developers hardcode values:

```css
/* Bad: values are hardcoded */
.button {
  background: #3B6DFF;
  padding: 12px 20px;
  border-radius: 8px;
}
```

With tokens:

```css
/* Good: values reference tokens */
.button {
  background: var(--color-primary);
  padding: var(--space-sm) var(--space-md);
  border-radius: var(--radius-md);
}
```

Change the token once, update everywhere. This keeps design and code in sync.

## Exporting Design Tokens from Figma

### Method 1: Tokens Studio Plugin (Recommended)

1. **Install Tokens Studio** (Figma plugin).
2. **Define tokens in Figma**: Create color styles, text styles, effect styles.
3. **Export as JSON**: Tokens Studio reads Figma styles and exports as `tokens.json`.
4. **Transform with Style Dictionary**: Convert JSON to CSS, SCSS, JavaScript.

```bash
# Install Style Dictionary
npm install -g style-dictionary

# Create config
cat > config.json << JSON
{
  "source": ["tokens.json"],
  "platforms": {
    "css": {
      "transformGroup": "css",
      "buildPath": "dist/",
      "files": [{
        "destination": "tokens.css",
        "format": "css/variables"
      }]
    }
  }
}
JSON

# Build tokens
style-dictionary build
```

Output: `dist/tokens.css` with CSS variables.

### Method 2: Figma Variables API

Figma's Variables API exports variables directly:

```javascript
// Requires Figma API token
const response = await fetch('https://api.figma.com/v1/files/:fileKey/variables/local', {
  headers: { 'X-Figma-Token': 'YOUR_TOKEN' }
});

const variables = await response.json();
console.log(variables);
```

Transform the response into CSS:

```javascript
const css = variables.variableCollections.map(v => 
  `--${v.name}: ${v.value};`
).join('\n');
```

### Method 3: Manual Export (Small Projects)

For small projects, manually copy Figma styles:

1. Open Figma file.
2. Go to Design Panel > Local Styles.
3. Copy color hex, spacing values, font specs.
4. Paste into `tokens.css`:

```css
:root {
  --color-primary: #3B6DFF;
  --color-background: #0A0D12;
  --space-xs: 4px;
  --space-sm: 8px;
  --font-size-body: 16px;
}
```

## Component Mapping

Developers need to know which Figma component maps to which code component.

### Figma Code Connect (Official)

Code Connect links Figma components to GitHub code:

1. **Set up Code Connect** in Figma (requires GitHub integration).
2. **Annotate components**: Map `Button/Primary` to `<Button variant="primary">`.
3. **Developers see code examples** directly in Dev Mode.

### Manual Documentation

If Code Connect isn't set up, document mappings in a README or Notion:

| Figma Component | Code Component | Props |
|----------------|----------------|-------|
| Button/Primary | `<Button variant="primary">` | `variant`, `size`, `disabled` |
| Icon/Home | `<Icon name="home">` | `name`, `size` |
| Card/Default | `<Card>` | `title`, `description`, `image` |

## CSS Variable Extraction

When Dev Mode isn't enough, extract CSS directly from Figma:

### Using Figma Inspect

1. Select a layer in Figma.
2. Enable Dev Mode.
3. Copy CSS from the right panel.
4. Paste into your stylesheet.

### Automating with Figma API

For batch export:

```javascript
// Fetch styles from Figma
const response = await fetch('https://api.figma.com/v1/files/:fileKey/styles', {
  headers: { 'X-Figma-Token': 'YOUR_TOKEN' }
});

const styles = await response.json();
// Process styles into CSS variables
```

## Developer Best Practices

When consuming Figma handoffs:

1. **Use Dev Mode**: Don't eyeball spacing. Copy exact values.
2. **Reference tokens**: Use CSS variables, not hardcoded values.
3. **Ask questions early**: If a spec is unclear, ask the designer before building.
4. **Test at multiple sizes**: Figma shows desktop; test mobile, tablet, and edge cases.
5. **Sync regularly**: Designs change. Re-export tokens and assets when designs update.

## Designer Best Practices

Before handing off:

1. **Use auto-layout**: Ensures spacing is consistent and measurable.
2. **Name layers clearly**: Developers see layer names in Dev Mode. Use descriptive names.
3. **Annotate edge cases**: Add notes for hover states, loading states, error states.
4. **Export assets at correct scale**: @1x for web, @2x and @3x for mobile.
5. **Publish design tokens**: Keep tokens.json or tokens.css up-to-date.

Figma Dev Mode, design tokens, and clear documentation turn design handoffs from guesswork into precision.

title: Create Accessible Color Palettes
seoTitle: Color Palette Management — WCAG Contrast, Perceptual Uniformity, Colorblind-Safe
seoDescription: Build accessible color palettes with WCAG contrast ratios, perceptual uniformity, and colorblind simulation. Export to design systems as CSS, JSON, SCSS.
content:
# Create Accessible Color Palettes

Color palettes fail when text becomes unreadable or colorblind users can't distinguish states. This guide covers WCAG contrast ratios, perceptual uniformity, colorblind simulation, and exporting palettes to design systems.

## WCAG Contrast Ratios

WCAG (Web Content Accessibility Guidelines) defines minimum contrast ratios:

- **AA (minimum)**: 4.5:1 for normal text, 3:1 for large text (18px+ or bold 14px+).
- **AAA (enhanced)**: 7:1 for normal text, 4.5:1 for large text.

Most products aim for AA compliance. AAA is recommended for high-contrast themes or government sites.

### Checking Contrast

Use a contrast checker:

- **Figma A11y Plugin**: Select text, check contrast against background.
- **Color.Ninja**: Paste colors, see contrast ratio.
- **WebAIM Contrast Checker**: [webaim.org/resources/contrastchecker/](https://webaim.org/resources/contrastchecker/).

Example:

- **Pass AA**: `#3B6DFF` (text) on `#FFFFFF` (background) = 4.51:1 ✓
- **Fail AA**: `#6EE7B7` (text) on `#FFFFFF` (background) = 1.78:1 ✗

If a color fails, darken text or lighten background until it passes.

## Building a Tonal Scale

Don't pick one blue and call it a palette. Build a tonal scale: 5–9 steps from near-black to near-white, tinted toward your brand hue.

### Example: Cyan Tonal Scale

```
cyan-50:  #E0F7FA  (background, hover states)
cyan-100: #B2EBF2
cyan-200: #80DEEA
cyan-300: #4DD0E1
cyan-400: #26C6DA
cyan-500: #00BCD4  (primary, base)
cyan-600: #00ACC1
cyan-700: #0097A7  (text on light backgrounds)
cyan-800: #00838F
cyan-900: #006064  (text, high contrast)
```

This gives you options: `cyan-500` for buttons, `cyan-700` for text on white, `cyan-900` for high-contrast text.

### Perceptual Uniformity

RGB space is not perceptually uniform. A jump from `#0000FF` to `#0000CC` looks different than `#FF0000` to `#CC0000`. Use **LAB color space** for perceptually uniform scales.

Tools:

- **Figma Palette Plugin**: Generates perceptually uniform scales.
- **Leonardo** (Adobe): [leonardocolor.io](https://leonardocolor.io/). Creates accessible, perceptually uniform palettes.
- **Coolors**: [coolors.co](https://coolors.co/). Quick palette generation with contrast checks.

These tools ensure each step in your scale has consistent perceived lightness.

## Colorblind Simulation

8% of men and 0.5% of women have color vision deficiency. Three common types:

- **Deuteranopia**: Red-green confusion (most common).
- **Protanopia**: Similar to Deuteranopia, but red is darker.
- **Tritanopia**: Blue-yellow confusion (rare).

### Testing Your Palette

Use colorblind simulators:

- **Figma Stark Plugin**: Simulate colorblindness in Figma. See how your design looks to colorblind users.
- **Color Oracle**: [colororacle.org](https://colororacle.org/). Desktop app that simulates colorblindness across your entire screen.
- **Chrome DevTools**: Open DevTools > Rendering > Emulate vision deficiencies.

### Fixing Colorblind Issues

Don't rely on color alone to convey information. Examples:

**Bad**: Green button = success, red button = error (colorblind users can't distinguish).

**Good**: Green button + checkmark icon = success, red button + X icon = error. Color + icon/text ensures clarity.

**Bad**: Red line and green line on a chart (colorblind users see two similar lines).

**Good**: Red solid line and green dashed line. Pattern + color ensures distinction.

## Exporting Palettes to Design Systems

Once your palette is finalized, export it as JSON, CSS, or SCSS.

### JSON Export

```json
{
  "colors": {
    "primary": {
      "50": "#E0F7FA",
      "500": "#00BCD4",
      "700": "#0097A7",
      "900": "#006064"
    },
    "background": {
      "default": "#0A0D12",
      "card": "#0F131C",
      "elevated": "#161D2B"
    },
    "text": {
      "primary": "#FFFFFF",
      "secondary": "#A0A4A8",
      "muted": "#6B7280"
    }
  }
}
```

### CSS Variables

```css
:root {
  --color-primary-50: #E0F7FA;
  --color-primary-500: #00BCD4;
  --color-primary-700: #0097A7;
  --color-primary-900: #006064;

  --color-background-default: #0A0D12;
  --color-background-card: #0F131C;

  --color-text-primary: #FFFFFF;
  --color-text-secondary: #A0A4A8;
}
```

### SCSS Variables

```scss
$color-primary-50: #E0F7FA;
$color-primary-500: #00BCD4;
$color-primary-700: #0097A7;
$color-primary-900: #006064;

$color-background-default: #0A0D12;
$color-background-card: #0F131C;

$color-text-primary: #FFFFFF;
$color-text-secondary: #A0A4A8;
```

Use a tool like **Style Dictionary** to automate conversion:

```bash
# Install
npm install -g style-dictionary

# Build
style-dictionary build --config config.json
```

## Naming Color Tokens

Avoid literal names (`blue-500`). Use semantic names:

- **Good**: `--color-primary`, `--color-background`, `--color-text-primary`
- **Bad**: `--blue-500`, `--gray-800`, `--cyan-700`

Semantic names let you swap colors without renaming every variable. If you rebrand from blue to purple, `--color-primary` stays the same; only its value changes.

## Testing Accessibility

Before launch:

1. **Contrast check**: All text passes WCAG AA (4.5:1 for normal, 3:1 for large).
2. **Colorblind simulation**: Test with Stark or Color Oracle. Ensure critical UI is distinguishable.
3. **Automated audit**: Run Lighthouse or Axe DevTools. Fix reported color contrast issues.
4. **Manual review**: Navigate the site without color. Can you tell success from error? If not, add icons/labels.

Accessible color palettes ensure everyone can use your product, regardless of vision.

# Sketch to Production Workflow

Transform hand-drawn sketches into production-ready digital assets with professional scanning, tracing, and cleanup techniques.

## Overview

Bridge traditional illustration with digital production through proper scanning, vectorization, and asset preparation workflows that preserve artistic intent while meeting commercial specifications.

## Scanning Phase

### Equipment Setup
- Use flatbed scanner at 600 DPI minimum for line art
- Set to grayscale or bitmap mode for clean captures
- Ensure clean scanner glass and proper lighting
- Use scanner holder or weight for flat originals

### Scan Settings
- Resolution: 600-1200 DPI for vector tracing
- Color mode: Grayscale for pencil, Bitmap for ink
- Format: TIFF uncompressed for editing
- Bit depth: 16-bit for maximum editing latitude

### Initial Cleanup
- Adjust levels to pure white background
- Increase contrast to isolate line work
- Remove dust and paper texture digitally
- Straighten and crop to artwork bounds

## Vector Tracing

### Illustrator Image Trace
- Import cleaned scan at full resolution
- Use "High Fidelity Photo" preset as starting point
- Adjust threshold to capture desired line weight
- Set Paths to 90%+ for smooth curves
- Enable "Ignore White" for clean backgrounds

### Manual Refinement
- Expand traced artwork to editable paths
- Use Direct Selection tool to smooth anchor points
- Reduce excessive anchor points with Simplify
- Refine curves with Convert Anchor Point tool
- Close open paths and fix gaps

### Detail Work
- Zoom to 400% for fine detail review
- Adjust overlapping paths and intersections
- Use Pathfinder to unite or trim shapes
- Add missing details manually with Pen tool
- Verify no stray points or artifacts remain

## Production Preparation

### Organization
- Create logical layer structure by element type
- Name all paths descriptively ("leaf-01", "stem-main")
- Group related elements into named groups
- Lock background reference layer if kept

### Color Assignment
- Apply appropriate color mode (RGB for digital, CMYK for print)
- Use global swatches for consistency
- Set spot colors if needed for screen printing
- Document Pantone references if applicable

### Quality Checks
- Verify all strokes converted to outlines if required
- Check for stray points (Select > Object > Stray Points)
- Confirm document color mode matches intended use
- Test at target output size for detail visibility
- Review at 25% zoom for overall composition

## File Export

### Vector Formats
- AI: Native working file with layers preserved
- EPS: Universal vector with fonts outlined
- SVG: Web-optimized with simplified markup
- PDF: Print-ready with bleeds and crop marks

### Raster Exports
- PNG: Transparent background at 4x target size
- JPEG: Solid background for photo contexts
- TIFF: Uncompressed for archival or further editing

### Production Package
- Include original scan reference
- Provide both outlined and editable text versions
- Add color palette documentation
- Include usage guidelines and size recommendations

## Best Practices

- Scan originals immediately while paper is pristine
- Keep layered working files separate from flattened exports
- Maintain consistent naming conventions across projects
- Archive original sketches and scans separately
- Document any manual adjustments for future reference
- Test outputs at intended production size before delivery

## Common Pitfalls

- Scanning at too low resolution limits tracing quality
- Over-simplifying paths loses artistic character
- Forgetting to outline fonts before final delivery
- Mixing RGB and CMYK in same production file
- Not preserving original sketch for reference

## Tools Integration

- Photoshop: Initial scan cleanup and raster prep
- Illustrator: Primary vector tracing and refinement
- Scanner software: High-quality capture settings
- Color management: Consistent preview to print

- Use contour for offset paths in sign design

- Link text frames across pages for long documents
- Apply columns within single frame
- Use baseline grid for vertical rhythm
- Import text from Word with formatting preserved

### Text Effects
- Apply drop shadows with interactive tool
- Use envelope distortion for dimensional typography
- Create outline text with contour tool
- Apply gradient fills to text
- Use PowerClip to mask images inside letters

### Import Options
- Import AI files with layers and effects intact
- Open EPS with font and color preservation
- Import DXF/DWG for CAD integration
- Link or embed images (TIFF, PSD, PNG)
- Maintain import source link for updates

### Export Formats
- PDF: Print-ready with bleed and color management
- AI: Adobe Illustrator with converted effects
- EPS: Universal vector with fonts outlined
- SVG: Web-optimized with clean markup
- DXF: CNC and vinyl cutter compatible
- PNG/JPEG: Raster with resolution control

- Outline fonts before exporting to AI or EPS
- Convert effects to objects for compatibility
- Flatten transparency for older PDF versions
- Embed color profiles in PDF exports
- Test imports in destination software before delivery

## Sign Design Workflows

### Vinyl Cutting Preparation
- Design with single spot colors per layer
- Convert all objects to curves
- Remove hairline strokes and fills
- Verify no overlapping paths of same color
- Export as DXF or EPS for cutter software

### Large Format Output
- Set document size to actual print dimensions
- Use high-resolution linked images (300 DPI at size)
- Apply appropriate bleed for trimming
- Use spot colors or CMYK consistently
- Include crop marks and registration

- Name layers and objects descriptively
- Group related objects for easier management
- Use symbols for repeated elements
- Save working CDR files with embedded fonts/images
- Test PowerClip edits at different zoom levels
- Convert effects to objects before cross-platform export
- Keep master elements on locked reference layer

- Close unused dockers to free memory
- Break apart large blends into static objects when finalized
- Use Outline view for faster editing of complex files

- Forgetting to embed images in final CDR file
- Using RGB for print-destined artwork
- Over-complicating paths with excessive nodes
- Not checking PowerClip contents before export
- Mixing measurement units within same document

- PDF: Can preserve some vector information if exported as artwork

### Optimal Export Settings
- Resolution: Export at actual size (300 DPI minimum for print)
- Color: Match intended output (RGB for digital, CMYK if converting later)
- Background: Include white layer, don't flatten alpha channel
- Bit depth: 16-bit if available for maximum color depth
- Format: TIFF or PNG for tracing, PSD for layer preservation

### File Organization
- Label exported files with clear naming (illustration-final-300dpi.tiff)
- Save multiple export versions if colors change
- Keep original Procreate file linked or annotated
- Archive high-resolution originals separately from working versions

## Vector Tracing

### Illustrator Image Trace
- Import cleaned raster into Illustrator
- Select artwork and open Image Trace dialog
- Try "High Fidelity Photo" preset first
- Adjust "Paths" slider to 90%+ for smooth curves
- Lower "Corners" value for hard angles (logos)
- Enable "Ignore White" to isolate linework
- Preview traces before expanding

### Affinity Designer Vectorization
- Import raster into Designer
- Use Studio > Image Vectorization panel
- Select "Accurate" for detailed illustration
- Use "Line drawing" mode for ink-based art
- Adjust quality slider to balance detail vs. smoothness
- Apply smoothing and simplification after conversion

### Illustrator Trace Enhancements
- Expand traced artwork to editable paths
- Select > Object > Stray Points to remove artifacts
- Direct Selection tool to refine curves manually
- Use Simplify command to reduce excessive anchor points
- Zoom to 400%+ for detail review of complex areas

### Manual Path Refinement
- Close any open paths created during tracing
- Remove overlapping paths that should be single shapes
- Merge small gaps or strokes that should connect
- Simplify paths while maintaining character
- Verify all fills and strokes apply correctly

## Color Application

### Spot Color Separation
- Assign traced paths to specific colors
- Use global color swatches for consistency
- Create separate layers per color for print separation
- Document Pantone references if using spot colors
- Test color output on target substrate

### Gradient and Shade Mapping
- Preserve gradient information from original illustration
- Apply linear or radial gradients to traced shapes
- Create color transitions with multiple overlapping shapes
- Use multiply or overlay blend modes for shadows
- Test gradients at intended output size

## Production Preparation

### Layer Organization
- Rename all paths descriptively ("eye-left", "nose", "mouth-shine")
- Group related elements ("face", "clothing", "background")
- Create separate layer for final line art if needed
- Lock reference layers or original raster
- Create export layers organized by output format

### Quality Assurance
- Check all paths for stray or hidden points
- Verify strokes converted to outlines where needed
- Test at zoom levels: 25%, 100%, 400%
- Check against original Procreate artwork for accuracy
- Verify no transparent areas in solid fill regions

### Scalability Testing
- Export at small size (icon dimensions) and verify legibility
- Export at large size and check for pixelation
- Test on different backgrounds and screen types
- Confirm effects (drop shadows, strokes) scale properly
- Document minimum size for acceptable reproduction

## Export Delivery

### Vector Formats
- AI: Native with full layer and effect preservation
- EPS: Universal with fonts outlined
- SVG: Web-optimized, clean code
- PDF: Print-ready with crop marks

### Multi-Resolution Assets
- 1x (100%) for standard display
- 2x (200%) for Retina/high-DPI screens
- 4x (400%) for print preview
- Export each as PNG, JPEG if raster needed

### Documentation Package
- Include original Procreate file for reference
- Provide color palette and Pantone references
- Document any custom brushes or techniques used
- Add usage guidelines (minimum size, clear space)
- Include layered working file separate from flattened export

## Best Practices

- Export from Procreate at full intended resolution
- Use high-contrast images for cleaner tracing
- Trace in desktop software (Illustrator/Affinity) rather than apps
- Create separate vector file per color separation if needed for printing
- Keep original Procreate file for future edits or variations
- Test final vector outputs on intended media before production

## Common Pitfalls

- Exporting too small from Procreate limits tracing quality
- Heavy texture or noise creates messy vector traces
- Forgetting to add white background before tracing
- Over-simplifying paths loses subtle curves and character
- Not testing legibility at minimum intended size
- Converting sketch layers directly without cleanup first

## Quality Troubleshooting

- Gaps in traced lines: Increase "Paths" in Image Trace or pre-process raster with Photoshop levels
- Over-complicated paths: Reduce "Paths" value or simplify after expansion
- Lost fine details: Increase export resolution from Procreate or trace sections separately
- Color shift: Check RGB/CMYK mode before tracing, correct in Illustrator after
- Pixelated curves: Export raster at higher resolution or manually refine paths post-trace

For illustration work targeting large formats, 600 DPI export ensures maximum quality.

faqs.answer: Both work well. Illustrator Image Trace excels at photographs and complex artwork. Affinity Designer's vectorization is excellent for line drawings and ink-based art. faqs.answer: Use Illustrator's Simplify command (Object > Path > Simplify) to reduce points while preserving curve shape. In Affinity Designer, use Select All and Curves > Smooth. Manually check the simplified result to ensure important details remain. You can also use the Reduce Nodes command in some Adobe plugins for more aggressive simplification.

# iPad Illustration Workflow: Digital Art to Multi-Format Export

Master professional iPad illustration workflows from concept and painting through multi-format export for web, print, and licensing.

## Overview

Create publication-quality digital illustrations on iPad with organized layer workflows, professional color management, and flexible asset export.

## Document Setup

### Canvas Configuration
- Create new document at intended output dimensions
- For print: 300 DPI, CMYK or RGB per final use
- For digital: 72-150 DPI at 1x, 2x, or 4x scale factor
- Set canvas size with padding around composition
- Enable grid overlay for compositional guidance

### Color Management
- Choose RGB for digital/screen (default)
- Choose RGB and convert to CMYK later for print (more control)
- Set display profile for accurate preview
- Create test swatches for spot color matching if needed
- Document color space decisions in document notes

### Layer Architecture
- Create base layer for white background
- Organize layers by major element groups
- Use descriptive layer names immediately
- Create folder hierarchy: background, characters, details, effects
- Keep linework on separate layer from color layers

## Painting Techniques

### Linework and Sketching
- Create sketch layer at lower opacity for composition planning
- Use low-opacity brush for initial rough laying out
- Build clean linework on separate layer above sketch
- Use monochrome or single-color brush for linework consistency
- Lock sketch layer after finalizing composition

### Base Coloring
- Create color layers grouped by region or character element
- Use flat colors first before adding variation
- Apply base colors on layers between sketch and detail
- Use clipping masks to paint within established shapes
- Create selection from linework layer to constrain color

### Detail and Texture
- Add midtones and shadows on separate layers
- Use overlay or multiply blend modes for shadows
- Use screen or add blend modes for highlights
- Build textures with dry brush or texture brushes
- Keep detail layers above base color for adjustment

### Effects and Atmosphere
- Apply lighting effects on top layer with low opacity
- Add atmospheric fog with large soft brushes
- Create depth with blur or desaturation of background
- Use dodge and burn techniques on dedicated layers
- Keep effect layers separate for easy removal or adjustment

## Color Refinement

### Hue and Saturation Adjustments
- Use Hue/Saturation adjustment layer for color shifts
- Adjust individual color ranges (reds, greens, blues separately)
- Use Curves adjustment for tonal refinement
- Create Levels adjustment for contrast control
- Keep all adjustments non-destructive with layers

### Color Harmony
- Use Color Dynamics panel to check color relationships
- Apply color picker to sample harmonious palettes
- Create swatches of dominant colors for reference
- Adjust saturation if colors appear muddy
- Check grayscale conversion for value consistency

## Performance Optimization

### Layer Management
- Flatten merged layers when detail phase completes
- Delete or merge duplicate or unused layers
- Consolidate similar layers to reduce count
- Archive high-layer-count versions separately
- Limit active layers to 20-30 for smooth performance

### File Size Control
- Work at 300 DPI only for final output
- Use 150 DPI for most digital illustration workflows
- Reduce colors in palette when possible
- Flatten background and non-editable elements
- Export to lower file size, keeping PSD as backup

## Pre-Export Preparation

### Final Composition Check
- Zoom to 100% and review entire artwork
- Check for stray marks or artifacts
- Verify colors are correct and consistent
- Confirm no unintended transparency or alpha issues
- Review against original concept or brief

### Layer Visibility
- Turn off sketch layers before export
- Hide reference layers or guides
- Show only layers intended for final output
- Test different layer combinations for variations
- Create separate layer sets for different export versions

### Color Profile
- Verify document is in RGB for digital export
- Assign sRGB profile for web export
- Create CMYK version for print output
- Embed color profile in exports if applicable
- Document color space in filename or metadata

## Export Workflows

### Raster Export Settings
- PNG: Transparent background, 8-bit or 16-bit per channel
- JPEG: Solid background, quality 85-95%, sRGB profile
- TIFF: Uncompressed or LZW, 16-bit for archival
- PDF: Preserves vector and raster information

### Multi-Resolution Export
- 1x (100%): Standard display size
- 2x (200%): Retina/high-DPI screens
- 4x (400%): Print preview or large displays
- Web optimization: Scale and compress for bandwidth

### Format-Specific Preparation
- Web: Scale to appropriate dimensions, convert to sRGB
- Print: Ensure 300 DPI at final output size, CMYK or RGB as specified
- Social media: Create versions optimized for platform dimensions
- Archival: Save as TIF or PSD with all layers intact

## Documentation and Delivery

### File Organization
- Save PSD with all layers as primary working file
- Export flattened versions for specific uses
- Create version-dated backups
- Organize exports by format and resolution
- Document color palette and any special requirements

### Metadata
- Add title, artist name in document properties
- Include copyright and usage rights information
- Document creation date and modifications
- Add color space and DPI information to filename
- Create README with file format descriptions

### Delivery Package
- Include original PSD with full layer history
- Provide all exported formats (PNG, JPEG, TIFF, PDF)
- Supply color palette as reference
- Add brief documentation of layers if complex
- Include lower-resolution preview for clients

## Best Practices

- Name layers descriptively from the start
- Use consistent naming conventions across projects
- Group related layers into folders
- Save frequently during long sessions
- Create backups at major completion points
- Test exports on multiple devices and screens
- Document color space and DPI in every export

## Common Pitfalls

- Working at too low DPI for eventual print use
- Creating too many layers causing performance issues
- Forgetting to flatten before exporting
- Exporting without verifying background transparency
- Not converting to sRGB before web export
- Losing original sketch and linework layers
- Assuming colors will match across different devices

## Troubleshooting

- Slow performance: Flatten merged sections, reduce layer count, work at lower resolution
- Color banding: Use Noise adjustment layer, increase color depth, check gradients
- Pixelated export: Verify export resolution matches intended use, resample at higher DPI
- Color shift on export: Check color profile assignment, verify document color mode, test on different screens

faqs.question: What's the ideal DPI for iPad illustration if I might print it later?
faqs.answer: Work at 300 DPI if print is primary use, or create at 150 DPI and upsample with Procreate's scaling for print. Most digital illustration works at 150 DPI fine for screen display. Keep the original high-quality PSD, and if print is needed later, you can always recreate elements at higher resolution or use smart upsampling techniques.

faqs.question: How should I organize layers for a complex character illustration?
faqs.answer: Group layers hierarchically: folders for Background, Character, Details, Effects. Within Character, subfold by body parts (Head, Body, Clothing). Use naming like 'head-skin-base', 'head-eyes-shine', 'head-hair-shadow'. This structure speeds editing and makes collaboration easier if someone else needs to adjust.

faqs.question: Should I paint with all layers at full opacity or use blend modes while working?
faqs.answer: Paint with layers at full opacity initially to avoid color confusion. Once base colors are solid, add new layers with multiply, screen, or overlay blend modes for shadow and highlight. This non-destructive approach lets you adjust or remove effects without affecting base work.

faqs.question: What's the best format for final delivery to a client?
faqs.answer: Deliver PSD (with flattened version), high-resolution PNG (transparent background), and JPEG (solid background). For print, add 300 DPI version in both CMYK and RGB. Include color palette documentation and usage guidelines. Provide lower-res preview for quick client review separate from production files.

# Design System Tokens: Building Scalable Design Language

Create comprehensive design system tokens to ensure consistency across all design and development touchpoints at scale.

## Overview

Design tokens abstract design decisions (colors, typography, spacing) into reusable, maintainable units that synchronize design and code.

## Token Structure

### Token Categories
- **Color**: Brand colors, semantic colors, state variants
- **Typography**: Font families, sizes, weights, line heights
- **Spacing**: Padding, margin, gap values in standardized increments
- **Sizing**: Component dimensions, width/height scales
- **Border**: Radius values, stroke widths
- **Shadow**: Depth and elevation patterns
- **Animation**: Timing functions, durations, easing curves
- **Opacity**: Transparency layers for hierarchy

### Semantic vs. Primitive Tokens
- **Primitives**: Base values (primary-blue-500, large-font-size)
- **Semantic**: Context-specific (button-background, text-muted, alert-error)
- Map primitives to semantic tokens for flexibility
- Use semantic tokens in components, primitives for theming

## Naming Conventions

### Structure
- Use kebab-case for token names (button-primary-background)
- Organize hierarchically: category/type/state/property
- Example: color/primary/on-dark/background
- Keep names descriptive but concise

### Color Token Naming
- Semantic: button-primary, text-secondary, border-disabled
- Tonal: color-neutral-50 through color-neutral-950
- State variants: hover, active, disabled, focus
- Example: action-primary-default, action-primary-hover

### Spacing Token Naming
- Use scale: spacing-xs, spacing-sm, spacing-md, spacing-lg, spacing-xl
- Or numeric: spacing-4, spacing-8, spacing-12, spacing-16, spacing-24
- Reference scale (4px, 8px increments for consistency)
- Example: spacing-md = 12px, spacing-lg = 16px

### Typography Token Naming
- By scale: text-xs, text-sm, text-md, text-lg, text-xl
- By use: heading-1, heading-2, body-lg, label-sm
- Include weight: text-md-regular, text-md-bold
- Example: body-lg = 18px / 28px line-height / 400 weight

## Token Organization

### Figma Tokens Plugin
- Install Tokens Studio plugin in Figma
- Create tokens.json file with organized structure
- Group tokens by category in plugin interface
- Define sets for light/dark modes
- Export as JSON for developer use

### JSON Structure
```json
{
  "color": {
    "primary": {
      "50": {"value": "#f0f7ff"},
      "500": {"value": "#0066cc"},
      "900": {"value": "#001a4d"}
    },
    "semantic": {
      "button-primary": {"value": "{color.primary.500}"}
    }
  },
  "spacing": {
    "sm": {"value": "8px"},
    "md": {"value": "12px"},
    "lg": {"value": "16px"}
  }
}
```

### Token Documentation
- Document usage context for each semantic token
- Explain when to use primitive vs. semantic
- Provide rationale for values (why 12px, not 10px)
- Create visual token library page
- Link tokens to components using them

## Theme Implementation

### Light/Dark Modes
- Create separate token sets for each theme
- Define theme-specific colors only (keep sizing consistent)
- Use token references to map between themes
- Document fallback behavior if theme switches
- Test contrast ratios for accessibility

### Multi-Brand Support
- Create token sets per brand if needed
- Override only brand-specific values
- Inherit common spacing and sizing
- Use consistent semantic naming across brands
- Document brand-specific decisions

### Platform Variants
- Create separate sets for web, iOS, Android if needed
- Use consistent naming across platforms
- Adjust values for platform conventions (larger touch targets on mobile)
- Document platform-specific overrides
- Keep consistent semantic structure

## Design System Implementation

### Component Mapping
- Apply tokens to all component variants
- Document which tokens affect which properties
- Create consistent interaction patterns via tokens
- Use semantic tokens in component main components
- Avoid hardcoding values in component fills

### Updating Tokens
- Change value in Figma token once
- All components referencing token update automatically
- Document change reason and date
- Version tokens for breaking changes
- Communicate significant token changes to team

## Developer Handoff

### Export Formats
- JSON: Raw token structure for custom processing
- CSS Custom Properties: --color-primary, --spacing-md
- SCSS Variables: $color-primary, $spacing-md
- JavaScript Objects: export const tokens = { ... }
- Format per platform and developer preference

### Export Tools
- Token Studio: Export to JSON, CSS, SCSS, JavaScript
- Figma Plugins: Style Dictionary, Tokens for design systems
- Custom scripts: Transform JSON to target format
- CI/CD integration: Auto-generate token files on updates

### Documentation for Developers
- Provide token JSON schema with examples
- Document how to reference tokens (CSS vars vs. imports)
- Explain semantic vs. primitive structure
- Include theme switching logic if applicable
- Provide fallback values for missing tokens

## Maintenance and Evolution

### Version Control
- Store tokens.json in version control
- Track token changes in commit history
- Mark breaking changes clearly
- Maintain changelog of token evolution
- Tag releases when major token updates deploy

### Governance
- Define process for proposing new tokens
- Require approval for token value changes
- Audit unused tokens periodically
- Document deprecation process for old tokens
- Keep design and dev teams synchronized

### Auditing Tokens
- Identify duplicate or redundant tokens
- Check for unused tokens and remove if obsolete
- Verify values match brand guidelines
- Test accessibility (color contrast, font sizes)
- Review for completeness against component needs

## Best Practices

- Start with primitives, add semantic tokens gradually
- Use reference values ({color.primary.500}) for DRY principles
- Keep token values aligned to project design specs
- Use consistent units (px or rem, not mixed)
- Document rationale and context for values
- Version tokens for major changes
- Sync design and code tokens regularly

## Common Pitfalls

- Too many tokens without clear organization
- Naming inconsistency across categories
- Hardcoding values in components instead of using tokens
- Not versioning tokens before breaking changes
- Forgetting to update documentation after token changes
- Creating tokens without developer input on format
- Over-abstracting with too many semantic layers

## Tools and Integration

- Figma Tokens Studio: Primary token management
- Style Dictionary: Transform tokens to code
- Storybook: Display token usage documentation
- GitHub/GitLab: Version control for token files
- Automation: GitHub Actions to publish updated tokens

faqs.question: What's the difference between primitive and semantic tokens?
faqs.answer: Primitive tokens are base design values (colors, spacings) with no context. Semantic tokens reference primitives and add meaning (button-primary uses the primary color primitive). Use primitives in theme definitions, semantic tokens in components. This allows flexible theming without changing component logic.

faqs.question: Should tokens be versioned or updated in place?
faqs.answer: For minor updates (color value tweaks within same scale), update in place. For structural changes or breaking changes (removing tokens, changing semantic meaning), version and communicate clearly. Track token history in version control to understand evolution over time.

faqs.question: How do I handle tokens for dark mode?
faqs.answer: Create separate token sets for light and dark themes in Tokens Studio. Define theme-specific colors only (e.g., text-primary is different, but spacing-md remains the same). Export both sets and let developers switch themes by swapping CSS variable values or token imports.

faqs.question: What format should I export tokens for developers?
faqs.answer: Ask developers their preference: CSS custom properties are standard, SCSS variables for preprocessors, JavaScript objects for framework use, or raw JSON for custom processing. Provide the format that best integrates with your development stack and tooling.

# Component Library Management: Building Scalable Design Systems

Build and maintain comprehensive component libraries that synchronize design and code for consistent, scalable digital products.

## Overview

Component libraries centralize reusable UI elements with clear variants, documentation, and code-to-design mapping for collaborative teams.

## Component Structure

### Component Organization
- Group by category: Buttons, Forms, Cards, Navigation, Feedback
- Create main component with all variants
- Use component variants for different states: default, hover, active, disabled, loading
- Create variants per size: sm, md, lg
- Document variant naming consistently

### Component Hierarchy
- Base components: Button, Input, Icon (atomic)
- Compound components: Form Group, Card with Header (molecules)
- Template components: Signup Form, Product Card (organisms)
- Page templates: Landing page structure
- Layer components logically for easy discovery

### Main Component Setup
- Set main component at page top with clear naming
- Include all possible variants in single main component
- Document which variant combinations are valid
- Use annotations for component behavior
- Lock main component to prevent accidental edits

## Variant Strategy

### Size Variants
- Small (sm): Compact UI, secondary actions
- Medium (md): Default, primary usage
- Large (lg): Emphasis, mobile-friendly
- Include all applicable sizes per component
- Document size use cases and contexts

### State Variants
- Default: Neutral, clickable state
- Hover: Mouse over or touch interaction
- Active: Pressed or selected
- Disabled: Non-interactive, grayed out
- Loading: Async operation in progress
- Error: Invalid input or failed action
- Success: Completed action confirmation

### Type/Role Variants
- Primary: Main action, emphasized
- Secondary: Alternative action
- Tertiary: Minimal appearance
- Destructive: Dangerous action warning
- Ghost: Minimal, background-only
- Document semantic meaning of each

## Component Documentation

### Design Specifications
- Document dimensions (width, height, min/max)
- Specify spacing (padding, gaps, margins)
- Detail typography (font, size, weight, line-height)
- Define colors using design tokens
- Explain animation behavior if applicable

### Usage Guidelines
- When to use this component (do's)
- When not to use (don'ts)
- Content guidelines (text length, image ratios)
- Accessibility considerations (contrast, keyboard, screen readers)
- Mobile vs. desktop differences if applicable

### Behavior Documentation
- Interaction patterns (click, hover, focus)
- Keyboard navigation (Tab order, Enter/Space triggers)
- Mobile touch interactions
- Error handling and validation display
- Loading and async states

### Best Practices
- Link to live examples or Storybook
- Include screenshot comparisons of variants
- Provide code snippets for common uses
- Document common mistakes to avoid
- Link to related components

## Design Implementation

### Using Main Components
- Drag main component into design file
- Switch variant in Design panel
- Override text content and images
- Document which overrides are expected
- Keep variant structure unchanged

### Detaching When Necessary
- Detach only when truly custom (rare)
- Document why detaching was necessary
- Consider adding new variant instead
- Sync detached custom components back to library
- Minimize detached instances for consistency

### Updating Component Instances
- When main component updates, instances auto-update
- Review and approve component changes before publishing
- Communicate significant changes to design team
- Update main component carefully to avoid breaking instances
- Use "Reset all changes" to revert overrides if needed

## Color and Typography Integration

### Token Application
- Apply design token colors to component fills
- Use semantic tokens (button-primary, text-muted)
- Link typography styles to token values
- Enable theme switching through token swaps
- Document token dependencies for each component

### Style Libraries
- Create shared text styles in Figma library
- Create shared color styles
- Document style naming (TextBody, ButtonLabel)
- Sync styles across component variants
- Version styles as library evolves

## Code Integration

### Design-to-Code Mapping
- Document component props in design annotations
- Map design variants to code props (size="lg", variant="primary")
- Document which props control which visuals
- Create component prop documentation
- Link design documentation to code README

### Code Connect (Figma)
- Use Code Connect plugin to link design components to code
- Map component instance properties to code props
- Generate live component documentation in Storybook
- Keep mappings synchronized with code changes
- Document mapping logic for maintainers

### Storybook Documentation
- Create story for each component and variant
- Include interactive controls to change props
- Document props with descriptions and types
- Add accessibility checklist per component
- Link to design in Figma from Storybook

## Library Maintenance

### Versioning Components
- Use semantic versioning (major.minor.patch)
- Major: Breaking changes (removed variants, prop changes)
- Minor: New variants or non-breaking additions
- Patch: Bug fixes or documentation updates
- Document migration path for breaking changes

### Publishing Library Updates
- Test component changes in staging environment first
- Get design and engineering approval before publishing
- Document changelog for each version
- Communicate breaking changes prominently
- Provide migration guide for major updates

### Deprecation Process
- Announce deprecation 1-2 releases in advance
- Provide replacement component or path forward
- Mark deprecated components in library
- Remove only after sufficient migration time
- Document deprecation reasons in changelog

## Audit and Evolution

### Library Audit
- Review components for consistency and quality
- Check for redundant or similar components
- Verify all variants are documented
- Test accessibility for each variant
- Validate token and style usage throughout

### Identifying Gaps
- Monitor new components created in projects
- Identify opportunities to extract reusable components
- Assess designer and developer feedback
- Prioritize high-value components for library
- Plan component library roadmap

### Performance Optimization
- Minimize component main files
- Archive legacy or rarely-used components
- Use copy strategy when variants diverge significantly
- Keep component count manageable (50-200 typical)
- Document reasoning for included components

## Best Practices

- Name components consistently and descriptively
- Keep component logic simple and focused
- Document all components, even seemingly obvious ones
- Version components and track changes
- Get stakeholder buy-in before major changes
- Test components across devices and browsers
- Keep design and code components synchronized

## Common Pitfalls

- Creating too many variants for edge cases
- Not documenting component usage or behavior
- Inconsistent naming across components
- Mixing design-specific and code-specific concerns
- Forgetting to deprecate old components properly
- Breaking changes without migration path
- Over-engineering components for flexibility

## Collaboration

- Use Figma Shared Libraries for design sharing
- Create public Storybook instance for developer reference
- Establish component review process
- Hold regular component library sync meetings
- Solicit feedback from design and engineering teams
- Document governance and decision-making

faqs.answer: Don't delete immediately. Announce deprecation in the next version with a migration path to the replacement. Keep it available for 1-2 more releases, marking it as deprecated in the library. Only remove after sufficient time for teams to migrate and after confirming no active usage.
